description: I’m Angelo, a full-stack web developer and I build with Python, Django, JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Bootstrap, Tailwind CSS and MySQL, and I like turning data into clean, useful dashboards.
summary: SPACE-PULSE is a health-monitoring web app for astronauts on long missions. Each crew member logs a short daily check-in. The app compares 7 health indicators against that person's own baseline: resting heart rate, heart-rate variability, resistance exercise, body temperature, sleep, mood and fatigue, and cabin CO2. It uses amber and red rules written by our Science Lead from published spaceflight research. When a value drifts, the astronaut gets a plain-language alert covering what changed, why it matters, what to do on board, and when to contact the flight surgeon. On a Mars mission a message to Earth can take up to about 22 minutes each way, so crews have to spot slow changes in their own health and act first. SPACE-PULSE puts that early-warning science in their hands and brings in ground support only when it matters. It's a labelled prototype that uses simulated crew data, not a medical device.
details:
What it does

- A dashboard with a 0–100 health score built only from the 7 Science Lead indicators. Each one has a 7-day sparkline and a status of Nominal, Caution, Critical or No data.

- Personal baselines computed from mission days 1–14, with a labelled manual override. Every rule is relative to the astronaut's own baseline, not a population threshold.

- 14 Science Lead alert texts, used word for word. Each says what changed, why, what to do, and when to escalate.

- A risk panel mapped to NASA's five Human Research Program hazards:

- Altered gravity: resting HR, HRV and exercise.

- Isolation: mood and sleep.

- Closed environment: CO2 and body temperature.

- Radiation: no dosimeter in the prototype, so it shows "No data".

- Distance from Earth: shows whether any alert calls for ground contact, next to NASA's published comm delay of about 3 to 22 minutes one way.

- Space-weather context from NASA DONKI (geomagnetic storms, solar flares, CMEs, SEPs). It's labelled as context and never enters the health score.

- Pulse, a rule-based health companion that answers questions like "why is my sleep amber?" from the statuses the app already computed. An optional language-model layer can only rephrase those answers, behind a validator that rejects any new numbers or diagnosis words. It's rate-limited per user.

- Pulse chat, a conversation panel with memory. Health questions are answered from the computed statuses, and urgent phrases such as chest pain or fainting go straight to a prompt to contact ground support.

- A ground panel for the comm delay. When an alert fires, it drafts a summary packet for the flight surgeon and shows NASA's 3 to 22 minute one-way delay, so the crew knows when to expect a reply and what to do on board meanwhile.

- A public read-only demo at /demo/. Each visitor gets a throwaway account with simulated crew data, nothing they do is saved, and live AI use is capped.

- A daily check-in, history charts (Chart.js), CSV import, alert acknowledgement, and a public /sources/ page that lists where every rule and number comes from.

Safeguards. We don't diagnose or infer hormones or mood, and we invent no thresholds. Every data source is labelled as sensor, check-in, CSV or simulated demo data. Experimental tiles are tagged and kept out of the score.

Built with. Python 3.13 and Django 6.1, Django templates, Tailwind CSS, Chart.js, SQLite, gunicorn and WhiteNoise, deployed on Render. More than 560 automated tests in Django's built-in test runner cover the rules, alerts, companion and pages.

Benefits and aims. It helps the crew catch slow, quiet changes early and act on board, and it cuts unnecessary calls to ground when every exchange is delayed. Next steps would be real wearable feeds, a radiation dosimeter input, and thresholds validated by a flight-surgeon review.
